title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 64
paragraphs: Matters of war are arranged among them thus. When a Scythian kills his first man, he drinks some of his blood; and of all those he kills in the battle he brings the heads to the king—for if he has brought a head he shares in the spoil they have taken, but otherwise not. He takes off the skin of the head by cutting it round the ears, then taking hold of the scalp and shaking it off. Afterwards he scrapes off the flesh with the rib of an ox, and works the skin with his hands; and when he has thus tempered it, he keeps it as a napkin for wiping his hands, and hangs it from the bridle of the horse he rides, taking pride in it. For whoever has the most skins for wiping his hands is judged the bravest man. Many also make cloaks to wear from the skins they have stripped off, sewing them together like shepherds' skin-cloaks; and many take the skin, together with the finger-nails, from the right hands of their dead enemies and make them into covers for their quivers. For human skin, it seems, is both thick and glossy, more brilliantly white than any other skin. Many also take the skins from the whole bodies of men, stretch them on pieces of wood, and carry them about on their horses.
